blocks.text: Candidate generation is neither unstructured brainstorming nor final selection. Produce a compact set in this dependency order:

items: State a simple correct reference mechanism so the computed relation and a small-input oracle are explicit.
Inspect that baseline for repeated work or missing structure, then add representatives that use genuinely different information or invariants rather than different syntax.
Attach each candidate's preconditions plus coarse preprocessing, per-operation, memory, and output costs so later evaluation does not have to guess why it works.
Hand the normalized set to legality rejection and comparative selection without declaring a winner during generation.

blocks.text: The order is causal: the baseline exposes work to replace, annotations require the candidate set to exist, and the handoff is evaluable only after those annotations are present. blocks.text: A meaningful candidate set should reveal the major strategy axes:

A one-pass hash set checks whether T − a[i] was seen at an earlier position before inserting a[i]. This prevents one position from pairing with itself and takes expected O(n) time with O(n) space.

Sorting creates value order. Two pointers at the smallest and largest remaining values move inward because a sum below T can only be raised by increasing the smaller value, while a sum above T can only be lowered by decreasing the larger value. Sorting dominates at O(n log n).

blocks.text: Candidate generation should expose alternatives whose preprocessing, per-query work, memory, or information requirements differ:

items: Direct scan: add a[l] through a[r] for every query. One answer costs O(r − l + 1) time and needs no index.
Full prefix array: define P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i], then answer [l, r] as P[r + 1] − P[l]. This uses O(n) preprocessing and storage, then O(1) time per query.

Offline boundary sweep: when all q queries are known first, sort their l and r + 1 boundary events, sweep the array once, and retain the running prefix total only at those boundaries. This uses O(n + q log q) time and O(q) boundary storage instead of an O(n) prefix array.

blocks.text: A for loop and while loop still implement the same direct-scan mechanism, while choosing only prefix sums hides the workload and storage boundary. The transfer rule is to generate one representative per materially different information and cost mechanism, with its preconditions, rather than one per coding style.

blocks.text: Candidate generation and final selection serve different purposes. A complete enumeration explicitly checks every legal pair, so it clarifies the answer contract and can act as a trusted reference: on small inputs, compare an optimized candidate's output with the enumeration's output to expose correctness bugs. Its repeated computations or searches also reveal work that a faster approach might replace with an index, ordering, or amortized state. The later feasibility gate rejects O(n²) work at the target maximum while retaining this explanatory and testing role. The transfer rule is to distinguish a reference candidate used to establish correctness from a deployable candidate required to meet the operation budget.

messages.text: The maximum constraints are part of the problem contract before implementation. Benchmarking can refine constants, but it cannot rescue a growth rate that exceeds the operation budget by orders of magnitude.

Correctness is necessary but not sufficient for the final strategy when the contract includes resource limits. The statement would be valid only for genuinely small bounded inputs where the quadratic cost fits.

feedback.reason: A slow but correct baseline can define semantics and expose optimization opportunities. Its presence as a reference does not make it feasible for deployment.
